title: Blocking Authentication Using Empty/Null Passwords for SSH
description: The PermitEmptyPasswords value allows for direct login through SSH without a password by a remote user/application to resources on the local host in the same way a standard remote login would. Permitting login without a password is inherently risky. Audit: PermitEmptyPasswords must be no or commented out (default no).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.11 Blocking Authentication Using Empty/Null Passwords for SSH

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # awk '/^.PermitEmptyPasswords/ { $1 = "PermitEmptyPasswords" ; $2 = "no" } { print }' /etc/ssh/sshd_config > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS # mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS /etc/ssh/sshd_config # svcadm restart svc:/network/ssh

title: Verify System Account Default Passwords
description: There are a number of accounts provided with the Solaris OS that are used to manage applications and are not intended to provide an interactive shell. These accounts are delivered either in a locked or non-login state. Oracle does not support nor recommend changing the passwords associated with these accounts. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.4 Verify System Account Default Passwords

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; command -v passwd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for user in $(logins -s | awk '{ print $1 }'); do [ "$user" = root ] && continue; stat=$(passwd -s "$user" | awk '{ print $2 }'); if [ "$stat" != LK ] && [ "$stat" != NL ]; then echo "Account $user is not locked or non-login."; fi; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Lock each listed system account with passwd -l <username>, or make it non-login with passwd -N <username>.

title: Ensure Password Fields are Not Empty
description: An account with an empty password field means that anybody may log in as that user without providing a password at all (assuming that the value PASSREQ=NO is set in /etc/default/login). All accounts must have passwords, be configured as "Non-login," or be locked. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.6 Ensure Password Fields are Not Empty

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { logins -p ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Use the passwd -l command to lock accounts that are not permitted to execute commands . Use the passwd -N command to set accounts to be non-login.

title: Verify No UID 0 Accounts Exist Other than root
description: Any account with UID 0 has superuser rights on the system. This access must be limited to only the default root role and be made accessible from the system console only. Administrative access granted to an unprivileged account should use an approved mechanism such as RBAC. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.7 Verify No UID 0 Accounts Exist Other than root

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { logins -o | awk -F: '($2 == 0) { print $1 }' | grep -vx root ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Disable or delete any other 0 UID entries that are displayed; there should be only one root account. Finer granularity access control for administrative access can be obtained by using the Solaris Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) mechanism. RBAC configurations should be monitored via user_attr(4) to make sure that privileges are managed appropriately.

title: Disable RPC Encryption Key
description: The keyserv service is only required for sites that are using the Secure RPC mechanism. The most common use for Secure RPC on Solaris machines is "secure NFS", which uses the Secure RPC mechanism to provide higher levels of security than the standard NFS protocols. ("Secure NFS" is unrelated to Kerberos authentication as a mechanism for providing higher levels of NFS security. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.4 Disable RPC Encryption Key

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/network/rpc/keyserv; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/rpc/keyserv

title: Disable NIS Client Services
description: If the local site is not using the NIS naming service to distribute system and user configuration information, this service may be disabled. This service is disabled by default unless the NIS service has been installed and configured on the system. As RPC-based services such as NIS may use non-secure authentication and share sensitive network object information with systems and applications using RPC-based service, NIS client daemons should be disabled. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant. If LDAP is not used, also confirm svc:/network/nis/domain is disabled.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.8 Disable NIS Client Services

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/network/nis/client; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/nis/client

title: Disable NIS Server Services
description: The NIS server software is not installed by default and is only required on systems that are acting as an NIS server for the local site. Typically, there are only a small number of NIS servers on any given network. These services are disabled by default unless the system has been previously configured to act as a NIS server. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant. If LDAP is not used, also confirm svc:/network/nis/domain is disabled.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.9 Disable NIS Server Services

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/network/nis/server; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/nis/server

title: Disable Telnet Service
description: The telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users from other systems via the telnet protocol and can be used for remote shell access. The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. The use of an unencrypted transmission medium could allow a user with access to sniff network traffic the ability to steal credentials. The ssh protocol provides an encrypted session and stronger security. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.12 Disable Telnet Service

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/network/telnet; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/telnet

title: Enable Auditing of Process and Privilege Events
description: The Solaris Audit service can be configured to record the use of privileges by processes running on the system. This will capture events such as the setting of UID and GID values, setting of privileges, as well as the use of functionality such as chroot(2). This recommendation will provide an audit trail that contains information related to the use of privileges by processes running on the system. The Solaris Audit service is used to provide a more centralized and complete window into activities such as these. Audit: each listed event must carry the cis class in /etc/security/audit_event.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 4.4 Enable Auditing of Process and Privilege Events

audit.command: [ -r /etc/security/audit_event ] || exit 1; r=compliant; for e in AUE_CHROOT AUE_SETREUID AUE_SETREGID AUE_FCHROOT AUE_PFEXEC AUE_SETUID AUE_NICE AUE_SETGID AUE_PRIOCNTLSYS AUE_SETEGID AUE_SETEUID AUE_SETPPRIV AUE_SETSID AUE_SETPGID; do awk -F: -v e="$e" '$2==e && $4 ~ /(^|,)cis(,|$)/ {f=1} END {exit !f}' /etc/security/audit_event || r="$e not assigned to the cis class"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: To enforce this setting, run the following commands to modify the /etc/security/audit_event file and add the cis audit class to the following audit events: # awk 'BEGIN{FS=":"; OFS=":"} {if ($2 ~ /AUE_CHROOT|AUE_SETREUID|AUE_SETREGID|AUE_FCHROOT|AUE_PFEXEC|AUE_SETUID|AUE_N ICE|AUE_SETGID|AUE_PRIOCNTLSYS|AUE_SETEGID|AUE_SETEUID|AUE_SETPPRIV|AUE_SETSI D|AUE_SETPGID/) $4=$4",cis";} {print} ' /etc/security/audit_event > /etc/security/audit_event.CIS # cp /etc/security/audit_event.CIS /etc/security/audit_event

title: Set Sticky Bit on World Writable Directories
description: When the so-called sticky bit (set with chmod +t) is set on a directory, then only the owner of a file may remove that file from the directory (as opposed to the usual behavior where anybody with write access to that directory may remove the file). Files in directories that have had the 'sticky bit' set, can only be deleted by users that have both write permissions for the directory in which the file resides, as well as ownership of the file or directory, or has sufficient privilege.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 5.1 Set Sticky Bit on World Writable Directories

audit.command: Perform the following to verify that the result is as recommended: # find / \( -fstype nfs -o -fstype cachefs -o -fstype autofs -o -fstype ctfs -o -fstype mntfs -o -fstype objfs -o -fstype proc \) -prune -o -type d \( - perm -0002 -a ! -perm -1000 \) -ls No output should be returned.

remediation.command: To set the sticky bit on a directory, run the following command: # chmod +t [directory name]

title: Restrict at/cron to Authorized Users
description: The cron.allow and at.allow files contain a list of users who are allowed to run the crontab and at commands to submit jobs to be run at scheduled intervals. On many systems, only the system administrator needs the ability to schedule jobs. Even though a given user is not listed in cron.allow, cron jobs can still be run as that user. Audit: cron.deny and at.deny must be absent, cron.allow must list root, at.allow must exist and be empty.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.3 Restrict at/cron to Authorized Users

audit.command: r=compliant; [ -e /etc/cron.d/cron.deny ] && r="cron.deny exists"; [ -e /etc/cron.d/at.deny ] && r="at.deny exists"; grep -qx root /etc/cron.d/cron.allow 2>/dev/null || r="root not in cron.allow"; if [ -f /etc/cron.d/at.allow ]; then n=$(wc -l < /etc/cron.d/at.allow); [ "$n" -eq 0 ] || r="at.allow is not empty"; else r="at.allow missing"; fi; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # mv /etc/cron.deny /etc/cron.deny.cis # mv /etc/at.deny /etc/at.deny.cis # echo root > /etc/cron.allow # cp /dev/null at.allow # chown root:root cron.allow at.allow # chmod 400 cron.allow at.allow Note that the root/superuser is always allowed to use the at command and is not required to be specifically listed in at.allow.

title: Disable Rhost-based Authentication for SSH
description: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that existing .rhosts and .shosts files, which may apply to application rather than user logins, will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication. Setting this parameter forces users to enter a password when authenticating with SSH. Audit: IgnoreRhosts must not be set to no (the default is yes).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.7 Disable Rhost-based Authentication for SSH

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # awk '/^IgnoreRhosts/ { $2 = "yes" } { print }' /etc/ssh/sshd_config > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS # mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS /etc/ssh/sshd_config # svcadm restart svc:/network/ssh This action will only set the IgnoreRhosts line if it already exists in the file to ensure that it is set to the proper value. If the IgnoreRhosts line does not exist in the file, the default setting of Yes is automatically used, so no additional changes are needed.

title: Restrict FTP Use
description: If FTP is permitted to be used on the system, the file /etc/ftpd/ftpusers is used to specify a list of users who are not allowed to access the system via FTP. FTP is an old and insecure protocol that transfers files and credentials in clear text and can be replaced by using sftp. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.8 Restrict FTP Use

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for user in $(logins -s | awk '{ print $1 }') aiuser noaccess nobody nobody4; do grep -w "$user" /etc/ftpd/ftpusers >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "User $user not in /etc/ftpd/ftpusers."; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/ftpd # cp ftpusers ftpusers.orig # for user in `logins -s | awk '{ print $1 }'` aiuser noaccess nobody nobody4; do $(echo $user >> ftpusers) done # sort -u ftpusers > ftpusers.CIS # mv ftpusers.CIS ftpusers If your site policy states that users have to be authorized to use FTP, consider placing all users in the /etc/ftpd/ftpusers file and then explicitly removing those who are permitted to use the service. To accomplish this, use the command: # getent passwd | cut -f1 -d":" > /etc/ftpd/ftpusers This prohibits any user on the system from using ftp unless they are explicitly removed from the file. Note that this file will need to be updated as users are added to or removed from the system.

title: Disable root login for SSH
description: The PermitRootLogin value (in /etc/ssh/sshd_config) allows for direct root login by a remote user/application to resources on the local host. By default, it is not possible for the root account to log directly into the system console because the account is configured as a role. Audit: pattern match on /etc/ssh/sshd_config as described in the CIS audit procedure.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.9 Disable root login for SSH

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # awk '/^PermitRootLogin/ { $2 = "no" } { print }' /etc/ssh/sshd_config > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS # mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS /etc/ssh/sshd_config # svcadm restart svc:/network/ssh

title: Disable Host-based Authentication for Login-based Services
description: The .rhosts files are used for automatic login to remote hosts and contain username and hostname combinations. The .rhosts files are unencrypted (usually group- or world-readable) and present a serious risk in that a malicious user could use the information within to gain access to a remote host with the privileges of the original application or user. Audit: no uncommented pam_rhosts_auth entry may exist in /etc/pam.conf or /etc/pam.d/*.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.10 Disable Host-based Authentication for Login-based Services

audit.command: command -v grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { grep -h pam_rhosts_auth /etc/pam.conf /etc/pam.d/* | grep -v "^[[:blank:]]*#" ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Edit /etc/pam.conf and any /etc/pam.d/* results from audit procedure and comment out or remove any pam_rhosts_auth lines: #rlogin auth sufficient pam_rhosts_auth.so.1 #rsh auth sufficient pam_rhosts_auth.so.1

title: Disable "nobody" Access for RPC Encryption Key Storage Service
description: This action listed prevents keyserv from using default keys for the nobody user, effectively stopping the nobody user from accessing information via Secure RPC. If login by the user nobody is allowed for secure RPC, there is an increased risk of system compromise. Audit: compliant when keyserv is not installed.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.14 Disable "nobody" Access for RPC Encryption Key Storage Service

audit.command: f=/etc/default/keyserv; [ -f "$f" ] || { echo compliant; exit 0; }; grep -q "^ENABLE_NOBODY_KEYS=NO" "$f" && echo compliant || echo "ENABLE_NOBODY_KEYS is not NO"

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/default # cp keyserv keyserv.orig # awk '/ENABLE_NOBODY_KEYS=/ { $1 = "ENABLE_NOBODY_KEYS=NO" } { print }' keyserv > keyserv.CIS # mv keyserv.CIS keyserv

title: Restrict root Login to System Console
description: Privileged access to the system via root must be accountable to a particular user. Use an authorized mechanism such as RBAC and the su command to provide administrative access to unprivileged accounts. These mechanisms provide an audit trail in the event of problems. Audit: pattern match on /etc/default/login as described in the CIS audit procedure.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.16 Restrict root Login to System Console

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/default # awk '/CONSOLE=/ { print "CONSOLE=/dev/console"; next }; { print }' login > login.CIS # mv login.CIS login

title: Set Password Expiration Parameters on Active Accounts
description: The characteristics of an operating system that make 'user identification' via password a secure and workable solution is the combination of settings chosen. The commands for this item set all active accounts (except the root account) to force password changes every 91 days (13 weeks), and then prevent password changes for seven days (one week), thereafter. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 7.1 Set Password Expiration Parameters on Active Accounts

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { logins -ox | awk -F: '( $1 != "root" && $8 != "LK" && $8 != "NL" && ( $10 < 7 || $11 > 91 || $12 < 7 )) { print }'; grep -q "^MAXWEEKS=13$" /etc/default/passwd || echo "MAXWEEKS is not 13"; grep -q "^MINWEEKS=1$" /etc/default/passwd || echo "MINWEEKS is not 1"; grep -q "^WARNWEEKS=4$" /etc/default/passwd || echo "WARNWEEKS is not 4" ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # logins -ox | awk -F: '($1 == "root" || $8 == "LK" || $8 == "NL") { next } ; { cmd = "passwd" } ; ($11 < 91) { cmd = cmd " -x 91" } ($10 < 7) { cmd = cmd " -n 7" } ($12 < 28) { cmd = cmd " -w 28" } (cmd != "passwd") { print cmd " " $1 }' > /etc/CISupd_accounts # /sbin/sh /etc/CISupd_accounts # rm -f /etc/CISupd_accounts # cd /etc/default # cp passwd passwd.orig # grep -v WEEKS passwd > passwd.CIS # cat <<EODefaults >> passwd.CIS MAXWEEKS=13 MINWEEKS=1 WARNWEEKS=1 EODefaults # mv passwd.CIS passwd

title: Set Strong Password Creation Policies
description: The variables in the /etc/default/passwd file indicate various strategies for creating differences required between an old and a new password. Administrators may wish to add site-specific dictionaries to the DICTIONLIST parameter. Warning: Sites often have differing opinions on the optimal value of the HISTORY parameter (how many previous passwords to remember per user in order to prevent re- use). Audit: /etc/default/passwd must set PASSLENGTH>=14, NAMECHECK=YES, HISTORY>=10, MINDIFF>=3, MINUPPER/MINLOWER/MINSPECIAL/MINDIGIT>=1, MAXREPEATS=1, WHITESPACE=YES and the dictionary settings.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 7.2 Set Strong Password Creation Policies

audit.command: out=$(cat /etc/default/passwd 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^PASSLENGTH=(1[4-9]|[2-9][0-9])$' '^NAMECHECK=YES$' '^HISTORY=(1[0-9]|2[0-6])$' '^MINDIFF=([3-9]|[1-9][0-9])$' '^MINUPPER=[1-9]' '^MINLOWER=[1-9]' '^MINSPECIAL=[1-9]' '^MINDIGIT=[1-9]' '^MAXREPEATS=1$' '^WHITESPACE=YES$' '^DICTIONDBDIR=/var/passwd$' '^DICTIONLIST=/usr/share/lib/dict/words$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq -- "$p" || r="missing: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/default # awk '/PASSLENGTH=/ { $1 = "PASSLENGTH=14" }; /NAMECHECK=/ { $1 = "NAMECHECK=YES" }; /HISTORY=/ { $1 = "HISTORY=10" }; /MINDIFF=/ { $1 = "MINDIFF=3" }; /MINUPPER=/ { $1 = "MINUPPER=1" }; /MINLOWER=/ { $1 = "MINLOWER=1" }; /MINSPECIAL=/ { $1 = "MINSPECIAL=1" }; /MINDIGIT=/ { $1 = "MINDIGIT=1" }; /MAXREPEATS=/ { $1 = "MAXREPEATS=1" }; /WHITESPACE=/ { $1 = "WHITESPACE=YES" }; /DICTIONDBDIR=/ { $1 = "DICTIONDBDIR=/var/passwd" }; /DICTIONLIST=/ { $1 = "DICTIONLIST=/usr/share/lib/dict/words" }; { print }' passwd > passwd.CIS # mv passwd.CIS passwd

title: Set Default File Creation Mask for FTP Users
description: If FTP is permitted, set a strong, default file creation mask to apply to files created by the FTP server. Many users assume that the FTP server will use their system file creation mask; generally it does not. This setting ensures that files transmitted over FTP use a strong file creation mask. Audit: only evaluated where the FTP server is installed.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 7.4 Set Default File Creation Mask for FTP Users

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc # if [ "`grep '^Umask' proftpd.conf`" ]; then awk '/^Umask/ { $2 = "027" } { print }' proftpd.conf > proftpd.conf.CIS mv proftpd.conf.CIS proftpd.conf else echo "Umask 027" >> proftpd.conf fi

title: Ensure root PATH Integrity
description: The root user can execute any command on the system and could be tricked into executing programs if the PATH is not set correctly. Including the current working directory (.) or any other writable directory in root's executable path makes it likely that an attacker can gain superuser access by forcing an administrator operating as root to execute a malcode, such as a Trojan horse program. Audit: root's login PATH must not contain ::, a trailing :, '.', or group/other writable directories.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.8 Ensure root PATH Integrity

audit.command: p=$(su - root -c 'echo $PATH' 2>/dev/null | tail -n 1); [ -n "$p" ] || exit 1; r=compliant; case "$p" in *::*) r="Empty Directory in PATH (::)";; *:) r="Trailing : in PATH";; esac; IFS=:; set -- $p; unset IFS; for d in "$@"; do [ "$d" = . ] && r="PATH contains ."; if [ -d "$d" ]; then s=$(ls -ld "$d/" | awk 'substr($1,6,1)!="-" {print "Group Write permission set on directory"} substr($1,9,1)!="-" {print "Other Write permission set on directory"}' | head -n 1); [ -z "$s" ] || r="$s $d"; fi; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step.

title: Check Permissions on User .netrc Files
description: While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' .netrc files, the users can easily override these. .netrc files may contain unencrypted passwords that can be used to attack other systems. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.11 Check Permissions on User .netrc Files

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for dir in $(logins -ox | awk -F: '($8 == "PS") { print $6 }'); do find "$dir"/.netrc -type f \( -perm -g+r -o -perm -g+w -o -perm -g+x -o -perm -o+r -o -perm -o+w -o -perm -o+x \) -ls; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if any user .netrc files are group- or world-readable or writable, and work with those users to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Check for Presence of User .rhosts Files
description: While no .rhosts files are shipped with Solaris, users can easily create them. This action is only meaningful if .rhosts support is permitted in the PAM configuration. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.12 Check for Presence of User .rhosts Files

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for dir in $(logins -ox | awk -F: '($8 == "PS") { print $6 }'); do find "$dir"/.rhosts -type f -ls; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if any user .rhosts files are present in user directories and work with those users to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Check for Presence of User .netrc Files
description: The .netrc file contains data for logging into a remote host for file transfers via FTP. The .netrc file presents a significant security risk since it stores passwords in unencrypted form. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.19 Check for Presence of User .netrc Files

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for dir in $(logins -ox | awk -F: '($8 == "PS") { print $6 }'); do ls -l "$dir"/.netrc; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if any .netrc files exist, and work with the owner to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Find World Writable Files
description: Unix-based systems support variable settings to control access to files. World-writable files are the least secure. See the chmod man page for more information. Data in world-writable files can be read, modified, and potentially compromised by any user on the system.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.21 Find World Writable Files

audit.command: Perform the following to verify that the result is as recommended: # find / \( -fstype nfs -o -fstype cachefs -o -fstype autofs -o -fstype ctfs -o -fstype mntfs -o -fstype objfs -o -fstype proc \) -prune -o -type f -perm -0002 -print No output should be returned. Note: The script above does a file traversal of all files under the "/" directory, including NFS attached file systems, so running this search command may take quite some time.

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine the existence of any "write access" given for the "other" category (chmod o-w <filename>), and work with the owner to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Find SUID/SGID System Executables
description: The owner of a file can set the file's permissions to run with the owner's or group's permissions, even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for a SUID/SGID program is to enable users to perform functions (such as changing their password), which requires root privileges.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.22 Find SUID/SGID System Executables

audit.command: Perform the following to verify that the result is as recommended: # find / \( -fstype nfs -o -fstype cachefs -o -fstype autofs -o -fstype ctfs -o -fstype mntfs -o -fstype objfs -o -fstype proc \) -prune -o -type f \( - perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -print No output should be returned. Note: The script above does a transversal of all files under the "/" directory, including NFS attached file systems, so running this search command may take quite some time.

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine the existence of any set-UID programs that do not belong on the system, and work with the owner (or system administrator) to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy. Digital signatures on the Solaris Set-UID binaries can be verified with the elfsign utility, such as this example: # elfsign verify -e /usr/bin/su elfsign: verification of /usr/bin/su passed.

title: Ensure rlogin, rsh and rexec services are disabled
description: Legacy remote-access services transmit credentials in clear text. Each SMF instance must be disabled or absent (`svcs -H -o state`); an uninstalled package is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11 Benchmark - Disable unnecessary network services (verify section number for your release)

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=disabled; for f in svc:/network/login:rlogin svc:/network/shell:default svc:/network/rexec:default; do st=$(svcs -H -o state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f:$st" ;; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/login:rlogin svc:/network/shell:default svc:/network/rexec:default (or uninstall the package with pkg uninstall).

title: Use the Latest Package Updates
description: The Solaris 11 OS should be periodically updated to install or upgrade software packages that will enhance the security, reliability, and performance of the system. For the Solaris 11 OS, there will be no more software patches issued, but rather security and other improvements will be installed by updating one or more software packages.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 1.1 Use the Latest Package Updates

audit.command: To verify that the system is operating with the latest software updates, perform the following and verify that the result is as shown: # pkg update -n No updates available for this image. In addition, you can manually verify the update associated with the running system using the following command. The output of this command will indicate the operation system version and update number as well as the Software Repository Update (SRU) number. pkg info entire Name: entire Summary: entire incorporation including Support Repository Update (Oracle Solaris ... (full steps: CIS section 1.1)

remediation.command: Run the following command to refresh the package catalog, download and apply any available updates: # pkg update

title: Configure TCP Wrappers
description: TCP Wrappers is a host-based access control system that allows administrators to control who has access to various network services based on the IP address of the remote end of the connection. TCP Wrappers also provide logging information via syslog about both successful and unsuccessful connections.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.1 Configure TCP Wrappers

audit.command: Perform the following and verify that the result is as shown: # inetadm -p | grep tcp_wrappers tcp_wrappers=TRUE # ls /etc/hosts.deny /etc/hosts.deny # ls /etc/hosts.allow /etc/hosts.allow The following script will check whether TCP Wrappers is enabled for all TCP-based services started by inetd. Individual inetd services may still be configured to use TCP Wrappers even if the global parameter (above) is set to FALSE. To check the status of individual inetd services, use the command: # for svc in `inetadm | awk '/svc:\// { print $NF }'`; do val=`inetadm -l ... (full steps: CIS section 2.1)

remediation.command: To enable TCP Wrappers, run the following commands: 1. Create and customize your policy in /etc/hosts.allow: # echo "ALL: <net>/<mask>, <net/<mask>, …" > /etc/hosts.allow where each / combination (for example, the Class C address block "192.168.1.0/255.255.255.0") can represent one network block in use by your organization that requires access to this system. 2. Create a default deny policy in /etc/hosts.deny: # echo "ALL: ALL" >/etc/hosts.deny 3. Enable TCP Wrappers for all services started by inetd: # inetadm -M tcp_wrappers=TRUE To protect only specific inetd services, use the command: # inetadm -m [FMRI] tcp_wrappers=TRUE where [FMRI] is the service to protect. To enable TCP Wrappers for the RPC port mapping service, use the commands: # svccfg -s rpc/bind setprop config/enable_tcpwrappers=true # svcadm refresh rpc/bind To protect UDP and RPC-based services that are spawned from inetd, consider implementing a host-based firewall. Oracle Solaris PF firewall (a.k.a. PF) has replaced Solaris IP Filter (IPF) in Solaris 11.4. See firewall(5) for more information.

title: Disable Local-only Graphical Login Environment
description: The graphical login service provides the capability of logging into the system using an X-windows type interface from the console. If graphical login access for the console is required, leave the service in local-only mode. This service should be disabled if it is not required. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.2 Disable Local-only Graphical Login Environment

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/application/graphical-login/gdm:default; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/application/graphical-login/gdm:default

title: Configure sendmail Service for Local-Only Mode
description: In Solaris 11, the sendmail service is set to local only mode by default. This means that users on remote systems cannot connect to the sendmail service, eliminating the possibility of a remote exploit attack against some future sendmail vulnerability. Leaving sendmail in local-only mode permits mail to be sent out from the local system. Audit: nothing may listen on ports 25/587 except the loopback addresses.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.3 Configure sendmail Service for Local-Only Mode

audit.command: command -v netstat >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { netstat -an | grep LISTEN | awk '{print $1}' | grep -E "\.(25|587)$" | grep -Ev "^(127\.0\.0\.1|::1)\." ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.guidance: Run the following to set sendmail to listen only local interfaces: # svccfg -v -s svc:/network/smtp:sendmail setprop config/local_only=true # svcadm refresh sendmail # svcadm restart sendmail

title: Disable Generic Security Services (GSS)
description: The GSS API is a security abstraction layer that is designed to make it easier for developers to integrate with different authentication schemes. It is most commonly used in applications for sites that use Kerberos for network authentication, though it can also allow applications to interoperate with other authentication schemes. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled or uninitialized; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.5 Disable Generic Security Services (GSS)

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/network/rpc/gss; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled|uninitialized) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/rpc/gss

title: Disable Apache Service
description: The Apache service provides an instance of the Apache web server. This service should be disabled if it is not required. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.6 Disable Apache Service

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/network/http:apache24; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/network/http:apache24

title: Disable Removable Volume Manager
description: The HAL-aware removable volume manager in the Solaris 11 OS automatically mounts external devices for users whenever the device is attached to the system. These devices include CD-R, CD-RW, floppies, DVD, USB and 1394 mass storage devices. See the rmvolmgr(1M) manual page for more details. Allowing users to mount and access data from removable media devices makes it easier for malicious programs and data to be imported onto the network. It also introduces the risk that sensitive data may be transferred off the system without a log record. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.10 Disable Removable Volume Manager

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/system/filesystem/rmvolmgr svc:/network/rpc/smserver; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/system/filesystem/rmvolmgr svc:/network/rpc/smserver

title: Disable automount Service
description: The automount daemon is normally used to automatically mount NFS file systems from remote file servers when needed. However, the automount daemon can also be configured to mount local (loopback) file systems as well, which may include local user home directories, depending on the system configuration. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 2.11 Disable automount Service

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/system/filesystem/autofs; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/system/filesystem/autofs

title: Disable Response to Broadcast ICMPv4 Echo Request
description: This setting controls whether Solaris responds to broadcast ICMPv4 echo requests. Reduce attack surface by restricting this vector used for host discovery and to prevent denial of service attacks. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_echo_broadcast` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.1 Disable Response to Broadcast ICMPv4 Echo Request

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ip; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_echo_broadcast -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_respond_to_echo_broadcast $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _respond_to_echo_broadcast=0 ip

title: Disable Response to ICMP Broadcast Netmask Requests
description: This setting controls whether Solaris will respond to ICMP broadcast netmask requests. Reduce attack surface by restricting this vector used for host and network discovery and to prevent denial of service attacks. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_address_mask_broadcast` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.2 Disable Response to ICMP Broadcast Netmask Requests

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ip; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_address_mask_broadcast -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_respond_to_address_mask_broadcast $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _respond_to_address_mask_broadcast=0 ip

title: Enable Strong TCP Sequence Number Generation
description: The variable TCP_STRONG_ISS defines the mechanism used for TCP initial sequence number generation. If an attacker can predict the next sequence number, it is possible to inject fraudulent packets into the data stream to hijack the session. The RFC 1948 method is widely accepted as the strongest mechanism for TCP packet generation. This makes remote session hijacking attacks more difficult, as well as any other network-based attack that relies on predicting TCP sequence number information. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.3 Enable Strong TCP Sequence Number Generation

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; grep -q "^TCP_STRONG_ISS=2$" /etc/default/inetinit 2>/dev/null || r="TCP_STRONG_ISS is not 2 in /etc/default/inetinit"; v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _strong_iss -co current tcp 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = 2 ] || r="_strong_iss current=$v"; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Set TCP_STRONG_ISS=2 in /etc/default/inetinit and run: ipadm set-prop -p _strong_iss=2 tcp

title: Disable Response to ICMP Broadcast Timestamp Requests
description: This setting controls whether Solaris will respond to ICMP broadcast timestamp requests. Reduce attack surface by restricting this vector used for host discovery and to prevent denial of service attacks. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_timestamp_broadcast` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.4 Disable Response to ICMP Broadcast Timestamp Requests

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ip; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_timestamp_broadcast -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_respond_to_timestamp_broadcast $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _respond_to_timestamp_broadcast=0 ip

title: Disable Source Packet Forwarding
description: This setting controls whether the IPv4 or IPv6 configuration will forward packets with IPv4 routing options or IPv6 routing headers. Keep this parameter disabled to prevent denial of service attacks through spoofed packets. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _forward_src_routed` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.5 Disable Source Packet Forwarding

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ipv4 ipv6; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _forward_src_routed -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_forward_src_routed $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _forward_src_routed=0 ipv4; ipadm set-prop -p _forward_src_routed=0 ipv6

title: Disable Directed Broadcast Packet Forwarding
description: This setting controls whether Solaris forwards broadcast packets for a specific network if it is directly connected to the machine. Keep this parameter disabled to prevent denial of service attacks. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _forward_directed_broadcasts` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.6 Disable Directed Broadcast Packet Forwarding

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ip; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _forward_directed_broadcasts -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_forward_directed_broadcasts $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _forward_directed_broadcasts=0 ip

title: Enable Stack Protection
description: Buffer overflow exploits have been the basis for many highly publicized compromises and defacements of large numbers of Internet connected systems. Many of the automated tools in use by system attackers exploit well-known buffer overflow problems in vendor-supplied and third party software. Enabling stack protection prevents certain classes of buffer overflow attacks and is a significant security enhancement. However, this does not protect against buffer overflow attacks that do not execute code on the stack (such as return-to-libc exploits). Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.7 Enable Stack Protection

audit.command: command -v sxadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sxadm status -po extension,status,configuration nxheap,nxstack 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^nxheap:enabled\.tagged-files:default\.default$' '^nxstack:enabled\.all:default\.default$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq -- "$p" || r="missing: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: To enable stack protection and block stack-smashing attacks, run the following: # sxadm delcust nxheap # sxadm delcust nxstack

title: Restrict Core Dumps to Protected Directory
description: The action described in this section creates a protected directory to store core dumps and also causes the system to create a log entry whenever a regular process dumps core. Core dumps, particularly those from set-UID and set-GID processes, may contain sensitive data. Audit: setid core dumps must be disabled, global dumps disabled or written under /var/share/cores, and /var/share/cores must be mode 700 owned by root.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.8 Restrict Core Dumps to Protected Directory

audit.command: command -v coreadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(coreadm 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq "per-process setid core dumps:[[:blank:]]*disabled" || r="per-process setid core dumps enabled"; printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq "global core dumps:[[:blank:]]*disabled|global core file pattern:[[:blank:]]*/var/share/cores/" || r="global core dumps not restricted to /var/share/cores"; s=$(ls -ld /var/share/cores/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1, $3}'); case "$s" in "drwx------ root"|"drwx------+ root") ;; *) r="/var/share/cores: $s";; esac; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: To implement the recommendation, run the following commands: # chmod 700 /var/share/cores # coreadm -g /var/share/cores/core_%n_%f_%u_%g_%t_%p \ -e log -e global -e global-setid \ -d process -d proc-setid If the local site chooses, dumping of core files can be completely disabled with the following command: # coreadm -d global -d global-setid -d process -d proc-setid

title: Disable Response to ICMP Timestamp Requests
description: This setting controls whether Solaris will respond to ICMP timestamp requests. Reduce attack surface by restricting this vector used for host discovery. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_timestamp` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.9 Disable Response to ICMP Timestamp Requests

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ip; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_timestamp -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_respond_to_timestamp $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _respond_to_timestamp=0 ip

title: Disable Response to Multicast Echo Request
description: These settings control whether Solaris responds to multicast IPv4 and IPv6 echo requests. Reduce attack surface by restricting this vector used for host discovery and to prevent denial of service attacks. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_echo_multicast` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.10 Disable Response to Multicast Echo Request

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ipv4 ipv6; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _respond_to_echo_multicast -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_respond_to_echo_multicast $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _respond_to_echo_multicast=0 ipv4; ipadm set-prop -p _respond_to_echo_multicast=0 ipv6

title: Ignore ICMP Redirect Messages
description: These settings control whether Solaris will ignore ICMP redirect messages. IP redirects should not be necessary in a well-designed and maintained network. Set to a value of 1 if there is a high risk for a DoS attack. Otherwise, the default value of 0 is sufficient. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _ignore_redirect` must be 1 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.11 Ignore ICMP Redirect Messages

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ipv4 ipv6; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _ignore_redirect -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '1' ] || r="_ignore_redirect $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _ignore_redirect=1 ipv4; ipadm set-prop -p _ignore_redirect=1 ipv6

title: Set Strict Multihoming
description: These settings control whether a packet arriving on a non-forwarding interface can be accepted for an IP address that is not explicitly configured on that interface. Enable this setting for systems that have interfaces that cross strict networking domains (for example, a firewall or a VPN node). Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _strict_dst_multihoming` must be 1 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.12 Set Strict Multihoming

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ipv4 ipv6; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _strict_dst_multihoming -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '1' ] || r="_strict_dst_multihoming $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _strict_dst_multihoming=1 ipv4; ipadm set-prop -p _strict_dst_multihoming=1 ipv6

title: Disable ICMP Redirect Messages
description: These settings control whether Solaris sends ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 redirect messages. A malicious user can exploit the ability of the system to send ICMP redirects by continually sending packets to the system, forcing the system to respond with ICMP redirect messages, resulting in an adverse impact on the CPU performance of the system. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p send_redirects` must be off for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.13 Disable ICMP Redirect Messages

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in ipv4 ipv6; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p send_redirects -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = 'off' ] || r="send_redirects $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p send_redirects=off ipv4; ipadm set-prop -p send_redirects=off ipv6

title: Disable TCP Reverse IP Source Routing
description: This setting controls whether TCP reverses the IP source routing option for incoming connections. If IP source routing is needed for diagnostic purposes, enable it. Otherwise disable it. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _rev_src_routes` must be 0 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.14 Disable TCP Reverse IP Source Routing

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in tcp; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _rev_src_routes -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '0' ] || r="_rev_src_routes $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _rev_src_routes=0 tcp

title: Set Maximum Number of Half-open TCP Connections
description: This setting controls how many half-open connections can exist for a TCP port. It is necessary to control the number of completed connections to the system to provide some protection against Denial of Service attacks. Note that the value of 4096 is a minimum to establish a good security posture for this setting. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _conn_req_max_q0` must be 4096 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.15 Set Maximum Number of Half-open TCP Connections

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in tcp; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _conn_req_max_q0 -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '4096' ] || r="_conn_req_max_q0 $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _conn_req_max_q0=4096 tcp

title: Set Maximum Number of Incoming Connections
description: This setting controls the maximum number of incoming connections that can be accepted on a TCP port. Note that the value of 1024 is a minimum to establish a good security posture for this setting. In environments where connection numbers are high, such as a busy webserver, this value may need to be increased. Audit: `ipadm show-prop -p _conn_req_max_q` must be 1024 for both the current and persistent values.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.16 Set Maximum Number of Incoming Connections

audit.command: command -v ipadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in tcp; do for k in current persistent; do v=$(ipadm show-prop -p _conn_req_max_q -co $k $p 2>/dev/null); [ "$v" = '1024' ] || r="_conn_req_max_q $p $k=$v"; done; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: ipadm set-prop -p _conn_req_max_q=1024 tcp

title: Disable Network Routing
description: The network routing daemon, in.routed, manages network routing tables. If enabled, it periodically supplies copies of the system's routing tables to any directly connected hosts and networks and picks up routes supplied to it from other networks and hosts. Routing Internet Protocol (RIP) is a legacy protocol with a number of security weaknesses including a lack of authentication, zoning, pruning, etc. Audit: ipv4/ipv6 routing and forwarding must be disabled both persistently and currently (routeadm -p).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 3.17 Disable Network Routing

audit.command: command -v routeadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(routeadm -p 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for k in ipv4-routing ipv4-forwarding ipv6-routing ipv6-forwarding; do l=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep "^$k "); case "$l" in *persistent=disabled*current=disabled*|*current=disabled*persistent=disabled*) ;; *) r="$k: $l";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: routeadm -d ipv4-forwarding -d ipv4-routing -d ipv6-forwarding -d ipv6-routing; routeadm -u

title: Create CIS Audit Class
description: To group a set of related audit events, the Solaris Audit service provides the ability for sites to define their own audit classes that contain just those events that the site wants to audit. To simplify administration, a CIS specific audit class should be created. Audit: pattern match on /etc/security/audit_class as described in the CIS audit procedure.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 4.1 Create CIS Audit Class

remediation.command: To create the CIS audit class, edit the /etc/security/audit_class file and add the following entry before the last line of the file: 0x0100000000000000:cis:CIS Solaris Benchmark

title: Enable Auditing of Incoming Network Connections
description: The Solaris Audit service can be configured to record incoming network connections to any listening service running on the system. This recommendation will provide an audit trail that contains information related to incoming network connections. Audit: each listed event must carry the cis class in /etc/security/audit_event.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 4.2 Enable Auditing of Incoming Network Connections

audit.command: [ -r /etc/security/audit_event ] || exit 1; r=compliant; for e in AUE_ACCEPT AUE_CONNECT AUE_SOCKACCEPT AUE_SOCKCONNECT AUE_inetd_connect; do awk -F: -v e="$e" '$2==e && $4 ~ /(^|,)cis(,|$)/ {f=1} END {exit !f}' /etc/security/audit_event || r="$e not assigned to the cis class"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: To enforce this setting, run the following commands to modify the /etc/security/audit_event file and add the cis audit class to the following audit events: # cp /etc/security/audit_event /etc/security/audit_event.orig # awk 'BEGIN{FS=":"; OFS=":"} {if ($2 ~ /AUE_ACCEPT|AUE_CONNECT|AUE_SOCKACCEPT|AUE_SOCKCONNECT|AUE_inetd_connect/) $4=$4",cis";} {print} ' /etc/security/audit_event > /etc/security/audit_event.out # cp /etc/security/audit_event.out /etc/security/audit_event

title: Enable Auditing of File Metadata Modification Events
description: The Solaris Audit service can be configured to record file metadata modification events for every process running on the system. This will allow the auditing service to determine when file ownership, permissions and related information is changed. This recommendation will provide an audit trail that contains information related to changes of file metadata. The Solaris Audit service is used to provide a more centralized and complete window into activities such as these. Audit: each listed event must carry the cis class in /etc/security/audit_event.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 4.3 Enable Auditing of File Metadata Modification Events

audit.command: [ -r /etc/security/audit_event ] || exit 1; r=compliant; for e in AUE_CHMOD AUE_CHOWN AUE_FCHOWN AUE_FCHMOD AUE_LCHOWN AUE_ACLSET AUE_FACLSET; do awk -F: -v e="$e" '$2==e && $4 ~ /(^|,)cis(,|$)/ {f=1} END {exit !f}' /etc/security/audit_event || r="$e not assigned to the cis class"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: To enforce this setting, run the following commands to modify the /etc/security/audit_event file and add the cis audit class to the following audit events: # awk 'BEGIN{FS=":"; OFS=":"} {if ($2 ~ /AUE_CHMOD|AUE_CHOWN|AUE_FCHOWN|AUE_FCHMOD|AUE_LCHOWN|AUE_ACLSET|AUE_FACLSET/ ) $4=$4",cis";} {print} ' /etc/security/audit_event > /etc/security/audit_event.CIS # cp /etc/security/audit_event.CIS /etc/security/audit_event

title: Configure Solaris Auditing
description: Solaris auditing service keeps a record of how a system is being used. Solaris auditing can be configured to record different classes of events based upon site policy. This recommendation will set and verify a consensus-developed auditing policy. That said, all organizations are encouraged to tailor this policy based upon their specific needs. Audit: checks audit condition, active policies (argv,cnt,zonename), user default flags (ad,ft,lo,ex,cis), non-attributable flags (lo), the audit_binfile plugin and root audit_flags; confirm the audit trail is growing manually.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 4.5 Configure Solaris Auditing

audit.command: command -v auditconfig >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; command -v userattr >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; auditconfig -getcond 2>/dev/null | grep -q "audit condition = auditing" || r="auditing is not active"; p=$(auditconfig -getpolicy 2>/dev/null | grep "^active audit policies"); for x in argv cnt zonename; do printf '%s\n' "$p" | grep -Eq "[=,][[:blank:]]*$x(,|$)" || r="policy $x not active"; done; fl=$(auditconfig -getflags 2>/dev/null | grep "^active user default audit flags"); for x in ad ft lo ex cis; do printf '%s\n' "$fl" | grep -Eq "[=,][[:blank:]]*$x[,(]" || r="audit flag $x not active"; done; auditconfig -getnaflags 2>/dev/null | grep "^active non-attributable audit flags" | grep -Eq "= *lo\(" || r="non-attributable flags are not lo"; auditconfig -getplugin audit_binfile 2>/dev/null | grep -q "audit_binfile (active)" || r="audit_binfile plugin not active"; userattr audit_flags root 2>/dev/null | grep -Eq "^lo,ad,ft,ex,cis:no$" || r="root audit_flags not lo,ad,ft,ex,cis:no"; echo "$r"

remediation.command: To enforce this setting, run the following commands: # auditconfig -conf # auditconfig -setflags lo,ad,ft,ex,cis # auditconfig -setnaflags lo # auditconfig -setpolicy cnt,argv,zonename # auditconfig -setplugin audit_binfile active p_minfree=1 # audit -s # rolemod -K audit_flags=lo,ad,ft,ex,cis:no root # EDITOR=ed crontab -e root << END_CRON $ a 0 0 * * * /usr/sbin/audit -n . w q END_CRON # chown root:root /var/share/audit # chmod 750 /var/share/audit

title: Disable login: Services on Serial Ports
description: The svccfg command provides service administration for the lower level of the Service Access Facility hierarchy and can be used to disable the ability to login on a particular port. Login services should not be enabled on any serial ports that are not strictly required to support the mission of the system. This action can be safely performed even when console access is provided using a serial port. Audit: `svcs -Ho state` must report disabled; a service that is not installed is compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.1 Disable login: Services on Serial Ports

audit.command: command -v svcs >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in svc:/system/console-login:terma svc:/system/console-login:termb; do st=$(svcs -Ho state "$f" 2>/dev/null); case "$st" in ''|disabled) ;; *) r="$f: $st";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: svcadm disable svc:/system/console-login:terma svc:/system/console-login:termb

title: Set EEPROM Security Mode and Log Failed Access (SPARC)
description: Oracle SPARC systems support the use of an EEPROM password for the console. Setting the EEPROM password helps prevent attackers who gain physical access to the system console from booting from an external device (such as a CD-ROM or floppy).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.2 Set EEPROM Security Mode and Log Failed Access (SPARC)

audit.command: Perform the following to verify that the result is as recommended: # eeprom security-mode | awk -F= '{ print $2 }' [command|full|none] # eeprom security-#badlogins | awk -F= '{ print $2 }' 0 If a password has been set, the command will return command or full. If a password has not been set, the command will return none.

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # eeprom security-mode=command # eeprom security-#badlogins=0 After entering the last command above, the administrator will be prompted for a password. This password will be required to authorize any future command issued at boot-level on the system (the ok or > prompt) except for the normal multi-user boot command (i.e., the system will be able to reboot unattended). Write down the password and store it in a sealed envelope in a secure location (note that locked desk drawers are typically not secure). If the password is lost or forgotten, simply log into the system and run the following command: # eeprom security-mode=none This will erase the forgotten password. If the password is lost or forgotten and this action cannot be completed, then the EEPROM must be replaced to gain access to the system. To set a new password, run the following command: # eeprom security-mode=command

title: Set Default Screen Lock for GNOME Users
description: The timeout parameter dictates the invocation of a password-protected screen saver after a specified time of keyboard and mouse inactivity, specific to the xscreensaver application used in the GNOME windowing environment. As a screensaver timeout provides protection for a desktop that has not been locked by the user upon his/her departure, to help prevent session hijacking, this value should be set as appropriate to the needs of the user. Audit: XScreenSaver defaults must set timeout 0:10:00, lockTimeout 0:00:00 and lock True (compliant when the desktop is not installed).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.4 Set Default Screen Lock for GNOME Users

audit.command: f=/usr/share/X11/app-defaults/XScreenSaver; [ -f "$f" ] || { echo compliant; exit 0; }; r=compliant; grep -q "^\*timeout:[[:blank:]]*0:10:00" "$f" || r="timeout"; grep -q "^\*lockTimeout:[[:blank:]]*0:00:00" "$f" || r="lockTimeout"; grep -q "^\*lock:[[:blank:]]*True" "$f" || r="lock"; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /usr/share/X11/app-defaults # cp XScreenSaver XScreenSaver.orig # awk '/^\*timeout:/ { $2 = "0:10:00" } /^\*lockTimeout:/ { $2 = "0:00:00" } /^\*lock:/ { $2 = "True" } { print }' xScreenSaver > xScreenSaver.CIS # mv xScreenSaver.CIS xScreenSaver

title: Remove Autologin Capabilities from the GNOME desktop
description: The GNOME Display Manager is used for login session management. See the manual page gdm(1) for more information. By default, GNOME automatic login is defined in /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin to allow users to access the system without a password. As automatic logins are a known security risk for other than "kiosk" types of systems, GNOME automatic login should be disabled in /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.5 Remove Autologin Capabilities from the GNOME desktop

audit.command: f=/etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin; [ -f "$f" ] || { echo 0; exit 0; }; n=$(egrep "auth|account" "$f" | grep -vc "^#"); echo "$n"

remediation.command: Comment out or remove all lines from /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin: # cp /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin.orig # awk '{ if ( $1 ~ /auth/ || $1 ~ /account/) $1 = "#"$1 } { print };' /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin > /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin.CIS # cp /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin.CIS /etc/pam.d/gdm-autologin

title: Set Delay between Failed Login Attempts to 4
description: The SLEEPTIME variable in the /etc/default/login file controls the number of seconds to wait before printing the "login incorrect" message when a bad password is provided. The default value for SLEEPTIME is 4 seconds. As an immediate return of an error message, coupled with the capability to try again may facilitate automatic and rapid-fire brute-force password attacks by a malicious user, this delay time should be set as appropriate to the needs of the user. Audit: SLEEPTIME must be 4 or left commented out (default 4).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.6 Set Delay between Failed Login Attempts to 4

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/default # cp login login.orig # awk '/SLEEPTIME=/ { $1 = "SLEEPTIME=4" } { print }' login > login.CIS # mv login.CIS login

title: Limit Consecutive Login Attempts for SSH
description: The 'MaxAuthTries' parameter in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted per connection. By restricting the number of failed authentication attempts before the server terminates the connection, malicious users are blocked from gaining access to the host by using repetitive brute-force login exploits. Audit: MaxAuthTries must be 6 or less, or commented out (default 6).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.12 Limit Consecutive Login Attempts for SSH

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # awk '/MaxAuthTries/ { $1 = "MaxAuthTries"; $2 = "6" } { print }' /etc/ssh/sshd_config > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS # mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS /etc/ssh/sshd_config # svcadm restart svc:/network/ssh

title: Disable X11 Forwarding for SSH
description: The X11 Forwarding parameter defined within the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file specifies whether or not X11 Forwarding via SSH is enabled on the server: The Secure Shell service provides an encrypted 'tunnel' for the data traffic passing through it. As enabling X11Forwarding on the host can permit a malicious user to secretly open another X11 connection to another remote client during the session and perform unobtrusive activities such as keystroke monitoring, if the X11 services are not required for ... Audit: pattern match on /etc/ssh/sshd_config as described in the CIS audit procedure.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.13 Disable X11 Forwarding for SSH

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.orig # awk '/^X11Forwarding / { $2 = "no" } { print }' /etc/ssh/sshd_config > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS # mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.CIS /etc/ssh/sshd_config # svcadm restart svc:/network/ssh

title: Secure the GRUB Menu (Intel)
description: GRUB is a boot loader for x64 based systems that permits loading an OS image from any location. Oracle x64 systems support the use of a GRUB Menu password for the console. The flexibility that GRUB provides creates a security risk if its configuration is modified by an unauthorized user. Audit: on x86 systems /rpool/boot/grub/grub.cfg must source password.cfg; SPARC systems are compliant.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.15 Secure the GRUB Menu (Intel)

audit.command: if [ "$(uname -p)" = i386 ]; then grep -q "password.cfg" /rpool/boot/grub/grub.cfg 2>/dev/null && echo compliant || echo "GRUB menu password not configured"; else echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: Run the following command to generate your password hash: # /usr/lib/grub2/bios/bin/grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 Enter password: Reenter password: PBKDF2 hash of your password is Create the file /usr/lib/grub2/bios/etc/grub.d/01\_password: #!/bin/sh /usr/bin/cat > /rpool/boot/grub/password.cfg< EOF /usr/bin/chmod 600 /rpool/boot/grub/password.cfg /usr/bin/echo 'source /@/boot/grub/password.cfg' Run the following to finalize the password configuration and set menu timeout: # /usr/bin/chmod 700 /usr/lib/grub2/bios/etc/grub.d/01_password # /usr/sbin/bootadm set-menu timeout=30 Changes will take effect on the next reboot.

title: Set Retry Limit for Account Lockout
description: The RETRIES parameter is the number of failed login attempts a user is allowed before being disconnected from the system and forced to reconnect. When LOCK_AFTER_RETRIES is set in /etc/security/policy.conf, then the user's account is locked after this many failed retries (the account can only be unlocked by the administrator using the command: passwd -u <username>. Audit: RETRIES=3 (or fewer) in /etc/default/login and LOCK_AFTER_RETRIES=YES in policy.conf; review exempt accounts (userattr lock_after_retries) manually.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 6.17 Set Retry Limit for Account Lockout

audit.command: r=compliant; grep -Eq "^RETRIES=[1-3]$" /etc/default/login 2>/dev/null || r="RETRIES is not 3 or less"; grep -q "^LOCK_AFTER_RETRIES=YES" /etc/security/policy.conf 2>/dev/null || r="LOCK_AFTER_RETRIES is not YES"; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/default # awk '/RETRIES=/ { $1 = "RETRIES=3" } { print }' login >login.CIS # mv login.CIS login # cd /etc/security # awk '/LOCK_AFTER_RETRIES=/ { $1 = "LOCK_AFTER_RETRIES=YES" } { print }' policy.conf > policy.conf.CIS # mv policy.conf.CIS policy.conf # svcadm restart svc:/system/name-service/cache Be careful when enabling these settings as they can create a denial-of-service situation for legitimate users and applications. Account lockout can be disabled for specific users via the usermod command. For example, the following command disables account lock specifically for the oracle account: # usermod -K lock_after_retries=no oracle Note: The root role is configured in this manner by default to prevent accidental lock out.

title: Set Default umask for users
description: The default umask(1) determines the permissions of files created by users. The user creating the file has the discretion of making their files and directories readable by others via the chmod(1) command. Setting a very secure default value for umask ensures that users make a conscious choice about their file permissions. A default umask setting of 077 causes files and directories created by users to not be readable by any other user on the system. Audit: UMASK must be 027 (or the stricter 077).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 7.3 Set Default umask for users

remediation.guidance: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # cd /etc/default # awk '/#UMASK=/ { $1 = "UMASK=027" } { print }' login > login.CIS # mv login.CIS login

title: Lock Inactive User Accounts
description: Guidelines published by the U.S. Department of Defense specify that user accounts must be locked out after 35 days of inactivity. This number may vary based on the particular site's policy. Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security since the users are not logging in to notice failed login attempts or other anomalies. Audit: the useradd default inactive value (definact in /usr/sadm/defadduser, shown by useradd -D) must be 1-35 days; check existing accounts with logins -axo.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 7.6 Lock Inactive User Accounts

remediation.command: useradd -D -f 35   (and for existing accounts: usermod -f 35 <user>)

title: Check for Remote Consoles
description: The consadm command can be used to select or display alternate console devices. Since the system console has special properties to handle emergency situations, it is important to ensure that the console is in a physically secure location and that unauthorized consoles have not been defined. Audit: applies to the global zone.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.1 Check for Remote Consoles

audit.command: command -v consadm >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { consadm -p ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Perform the following to implement the recommended state: # /usr/sbin/consadm [-d device...]

title: Check for Duplicate User Names
description: Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate user name, it is possible for an administrator to manually modify passwd(4) and change the user name. If a user is assigned a duplicate user name, it will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in passwd(4). Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.2 Check for Duplicate User Names

audit.command: command -v getent >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { getent passwd | cut -f1 -d: | sort | uniq -d ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if there are any duplicate user names, and work with their respective owners to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Check That Defined Home Directories Exist
description: Users can be defined to have a home directory in passwd(4), even if the directory does not actually exist. If the user's home directory does not exist, the user will be placed in "/" and will not be able to write any files or have local environment variables set. Audit: every account home directory must exist (uucp/nuucp are excluded as CIS notes).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.3 Check That Defined Home Directories Exist

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { logins -xo | awk -F: '{print $1, $6}' | while read user home; do [ -d "$home" ] || echo "$user"; done | grep -Evx "uucp|nuucp" ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if there exists any users whose home directories do not exist, and work with those users to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Verify System File Permissions
description: The pkg verify and command checks the accuracy of installed directory structures and files. It is important to ensure that system files and directories are maintained with the permissions they were intended to have from the OS vendor (Oracle).
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.5 Verify System File Permissions

audit.command: Perform the following to verify that the result is as recommended: # pkg verify Errors may be a simple reflection of changes made earlier in this benchmark, such as alteration of the ownership of the cron process, so this result indicates that pkg verify is doing its job and detecting file changes.

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Perform the following to set correct any identified package errors: # pkg fix Exercise caution in running this command as it may reverse modifications implemented previously including some of those recommended by this document. Rather than use this command broadly, it is recommended that it be used more tactically to correct specific package problems when possible.

title: Check Permissions on User Home Directories
description: While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' home directories, the users can easily override these. Group or world-writable user home directories may enable malicious users to steal or modify other users' data or to gain another user's system privileges. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.9 Check Permissions on User Home Directories

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for dir in $(logins -ox | awk -F: '($8 == "PS") { print $6 }'); do find "$dir" -type d -prune \( -perm -g+w -o -perm -o+r -o -perm -o+w -o -perm -o+x \) -ls; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if any user directory permissions are world-readable, writable, or executable, and work with those users to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Check Permissions on User "." (Hidden) Files
description: While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' "dot" files, the users can easily override these. Group or world-writable user configuration files may enable malicious users to steal or modify other users' data or to gain another user's system privileges. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS Oracle Solaris 11.4 Benchmark v1.1.0 - 9.10 Check Permissions on User "." (Hidden) Files

audit.command: command -v logins >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for dir in $(logins -ox | awk -F: '($8 == "PS") { print $6 }'); do find "$dir"/.[A-Za-z0-9]* ! -type l \( -perm -20 -o -perm -02 \) -ls; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Correct or justify any items discovered in the Audit step. Determine if any user hidden files are world-readable or writable, and work with those users to determine the best course of action in accordance with site policy.

title: Check Groups in passwd
